commitResults.messageTitle: Add Todo, Deadline and Event Task types
Fix input trimming and article in error messages
Save tasks to file whenever the list changes
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks are held only in memory, so the list is lost as soon as the
  program exits and the user has to retype everything on each run.

  Persist the list to ./data/harvey.txt after every command that
  changes it. Each Task subclass serialises itself through
  toFileFormat(), matching how each already renders itself through
  toString(), so adding a task type later means editing only the new
  class instead of a type check inside Storage.

  Loading is not implemented yet, so the file is written but never
  read back.

The task list is written to disk but never read back, so restarting
  Harvey still shows an empty list and the saved file is dead weight.

  Read the file in Storage.load() and start the list from it. Parsing
  cannot mirror the polymorphic toFileFormat(): there is no task yet to
  ask, so Storage reads the type letter and picks the constructor. A
  missing file means nobody has run Harvey here before, so it yields an
  empty list rather than an error, and a file that cannot be read is
  reported without stopping Harvey from starting.

  Lines that are present but malformed are not handled yet.

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle damaged lines in the saved file
commitResults.messageBody:
The save file is plain text that anyone can open and edit, but every
  line was trusted. A short line crashed Harvey with an array error
  before it could start, and an unrecognised type letter quietly became
  a Todo, turning damaged data into a wrong task. Task text containing
  the field separator was also written out and then silently dropped on
  the next run.

  Check the type letter, field count, description and done flag before
  using them, and reject anything unexpected. Damaged lines are skipped
  rather than treated as fatal, so one bad line does not cost the user
  the rest of the file, and Harvey reports how many were left out so the
  loss is not mistaken for an empty file.

  Refuse the separator character when a task is created. Failing at the
  moment the user types it is clearer than accepting the task and losing
  it an hour later.

A deadline held its due date as whatever text the user typed, so
  Harvey could only echo it back. It could not tell 2019-10-15 from
  tomorrow, and had no way to compare or sort by date later.

  Parse the date into a java.time.LocalDate when the task is created,
  accepting yyyy-mm-dd and displaying MMM d yyyy, so the shown form no
  longer has to match the typed one. Parsing lives in Deadline, next to
  the field it fills, so the command parser and the save file reader
  share one definition of a valid date instead of each having their own.

  The file keeps the yyyy-mm-dd form rather than the display form, so it
  can be read back by that same parser. A date that cannot be parsed is
  refused when typed, and skipped as a damaged line when found in the
  file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract user interaction into a Ui class
commitResults.messageBody:
Harvey does everything: it owns the banner and divider, calls
System.out directly, reads the Scanner, and also decides what each
command means. Changing the wording of a reply means editing the same
class that holds the command logic, and there is no single place to
look for how Harvey talks to the user.

Move all reading and printing into a Ui class. Harvey now asks Ui for
the next command and hands it messages to display, and no longer
mentions System.out or Scanner at all. Ui also owns the "Sorry! "
prefix through showError, so callers pass only the explanation and
every error reads the same way.

This is the first step towards the target design and the safest one to
do first, because Ui depends on nothing else in the program. Output is
unchanged: a scripted run of every command and error path produces
byte-identical text to the run before this change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract the task list into a TaskList class
commitResults.messageBody:
The tasks lived in a bare ArrayList that Harvey passed around. Because
the user counts tasks from 1 and an ArrayList counts from 0, every
command subtracted 1 by hand, and parseTaskNumber had to be told the
size of the list so it could check the number was in range. The rule
for what counts as a valid task number was therefore split between a
helper that did not own the list and the call sites that used it.

Wrap the list in a TaskList that offers add, get, delete, size and
isEmpty in the user's own numbering, and does the conversion and the
bounds check in one private method. Harvey no longer mentions indices
at all; parseTaskNumber is left with only the two checks that need to
know which command was typed.

Output is unchanged, verified byte-identical against a scripted run of
every command and error path.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract command interpretation into a Parser class
commitResults.messageBody:
Harvey both worked out what the user meant and carried it out. It split
the line into a keyword and an argument, decided which Command that
was, built tasks from the /by, /from and /to separators, and turned a
typed number into a task number. Those rules, and the wording used to
explain a mistake in them, were interleaved with the code that acts on
the result, so neither could be read on its own.

Move the interpretation into a Parser class: parseCommand,
parseArgument, createTask and parseTaskNumber, along with the /by,
/from and /to separators and the reserved | character. The methods are
static because parsing needs no memory of what came before. Harvey's
loop now reads as ask Parser what this means, then do it.

Output is unchanged, verified byte-identical against a scripted run of
every command and error path.

commitResults.messageTitle: Turn Harvey into an object and move list display into Ui
commitResults.messageBody:
Harvey was still a single static main holding local variables for the
Ui, the Storage and the task list, with the whole command loop and the
numbered-list formatting inline. Nothing could refer to Harvey as a
thing; there was only a method that ran from top to bottom.

Give Harvey fields for its three collaborators, a constructor that
builds them, and a run() method that drives the loop, so main() is one
line. Split the switch out into runCommand() and the file reading into
loadTasks(), so run() shows the shape of a session rather than the
detail of every command. Move the numbered listing into Ui.showTaskList,
since numbering is a display decision and TaskList has no opinion on
how it should look.

Loading stays in run() rather than the constructor, unlike the sample
design in the brief. A complaint about the save file otherwise prints
above the greeting, and a constructor that reads files and writes to
the screen is doing more than constructing.

Output is unchanged, verified byte-identical against a scripted run of
every command and error path, plus separate checks of the damaged-file
and restart-persistence paths.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename the Command enum to CommandType
commitResults.messageBody:
The next step is a Command class hierarchy, where a Command is an
action that can execute itself. The name is currently taken by the enum
of keywords, which is a different idea: it says which instructions
exist and how each is written, not what any of them does.

Rename the enum to CommandType so the better name is free for the
class that will carry the behaviour. This is a rename and nothing else,
kept as its own commit so the change that follows contains no noise.

Output is unchanged, verified byte-identical against a scripted run of
every command and error path.

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace the command switch with a Command class hierarchy
commitResults.messageBody:
Harvey's runCommand held one switch naming every instruction and
spelling out what each did. The switch grew a branch per feature, and
the code for one instruction was a fragment of a method rather than
something with a name that could be read, moved or tested on its own.

Add an abstract Command with execute(tasks, ui, storage) and isExit(),
and a subclass per instruction: Add, List, Mark, Unmark, Delete, Exit.
Parser.parse now returns the right subclass, so the main loop no longer
names any instruction at all: parse, execute, ask whether to stop.
Adding a feature means adding a class instead of editing a switch, and
the switch that remains is in Parser, whose job is choosing.

Two deliberate differences from the sample loop in the brief. Ui prints
its own divider after each reply, so there is no showLine() call before
and after in a finally; adding one would print dividers twice. And the
parting message stays in Harvey rather than moving into ExitCommand,
because it must also appear when input runs out with no bye typed.

Saving moved into the commands that change the list, which is what
passing storage to execute is for. ListCommand no longer saves; it
previously rewrote identical content.

Output is unchanged, verified byte-identical against a scripted run of
every command and error path, plus separate checks of the damaged-file,
restart-persistence and end-of-input paths.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organize classes into packages under harvey
commitResults.messageBody:
All eighteen classes sat in the default package, in one flat folder.
Nothing said which classes belong together, and a class in the default
package cannot be imported by a class in any named package, so the
layout would have blocked splitting the code up later.

Move everything under harvey, with one subpackage per role established
by A-MoreOOP: harvey.command, harvey.task, harvey.parser,
harvey.storage and harvey.ui. Harvey and HarveyException stay at the
top, the first because it wires the others together and the second
because every package throws it. CommandType goes with the commands,
since what it lists is the commands.

src/main/java remains the source root, as required; src, main and java
are not packages. The main class is now harvey.Harvey, so running it
by hand needs the full name:

  javac -d /tmp/out $(find src/main/java -name '*.java')
  java -cp /tmp/out harvey.Harvey

The move left harvey.parser and harvey.command importing each other,
because Parser builds the command objects while the commands call back
into Parser for the details of their arguments. This compiles, but the
cycle is worth removing; that is the next increment.

Output is unchanged, verified byte-identical against a scripted run of
every command and error path, plus the damaged-file and restart paths.

commitResults.messageTitle: Break the cycle between the parser and command packages
commitResults.messageBody:
Splitting into packages exposed a dependency that was invisible while
everything sat in one folder: harvey.parser imported harvey.command to
build the command objects, and every command imported harvey.parser
back, because Parser still held createTask and parseTaskNumber. Two
packages that need each other cannot be understood, moved or reused
apart, which defeats the point of separating them.

Move each piece to the package that uses it. createTask, splitAtOption
and the /by, /from, /to and | constants belong to AddCommand, the only
class that builds tasks from typed text. parseTaskNumber becomes a
protected helper on Command, shared by Mark, Unmark and Delete.

Parser is left with what its name promises: read the command word,
return the matching Command. It drops from 216 lines to 90, and the
dependency now runs one way, from parser to command.

An alternative was a TaskNumberCommand between Command and the three
commands that take a number, which would also remove their duplicated
argument field. That is a larger change than removing the cycle needs,
so it is left for later.

Output is unchanged, verified byte-identical against a scripted run of
every command and error path, plus the damaged-file and restart paths.

commitResults.messageTitle: Point Gradle at the Harvey main class
commitResults.messageBody:
The build file merged from add-gradle-support names the original
  starter class, seedu.duke.Duke, which does not exist in this project,
  so every Gradle task that runs the app failed immediately.

  Point mainClass at harvey.Harvey and name the shadow jar harvey.jar.
  Verified with gradlew build, gradlew run, and running the produced jar
  directly.

The project had no automated tests. Every change so far was checked by
running the chatbot by hand and reading the output, which is slow and
only covers whatever the person remembered to type.

Start with TaskList, because it holds the one piece of logic most
likely to be wrong and least visible when it is: the user counts tasks
from 1 and the list counts from 0. The tests cover both ends of the
valid range and both sides of each boundary, including 0, which is a
legal index into the underlying list but not a legal task number.

Also covered: that get returns the stored object rather than a copy,
since Harvey marks a task by mutating what get returned, and that
delete closes the gap so later task numbers stay correct.

Checked the tests are not vacuous by removing the "- 1" from toIndex
and confirming the suite fails, then restoring it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for Deadline, CommandType and Parser
commitResults.messageBody:
Extends the suite from one class to four, covering the three remaining
places where a mistake would be quiet rather than obvious.

Deadline: a date is written to the file in one format and shown to the
user in another, and one parseDate reads both what the user types and
what the file holds. If those stop agreeing, saved deadlines vanish on
the next startup, so the round trip is asserted directly. Also covered
are dates that are well formed but impossible, such as 2019-02-29,
which a check on the shape of the text alone would accept.

CommandType: the messages it produces are the ones users see most, so
the tests assert the unknown-word message quotes what was typed and
lists the commands. Two tests loop over values() so a command added
later is covered without editing them.

Parser: asserts which Command subclass comes back, not what it does.
Includes unmark, which shares a prefix with mark and would break if the
keyword were ever matched by startsWith rather than equality, and a
command typed with no argument, which the parser should still accept
and leave for the command itself to reject.

43 tests, all passing under gradlew test.

Storage was the largest untested class and the one whose failures are
hardest to notice: a fault here loses the user's tasks quietly, between
one run and the next, with nothing shown on screen.

The tests use JUnit's @TempDir so each one gets its own empty folder,
which keeps them independent and stops them touching the real
./data/harvey.txt. They write and read actual files rather than a fake
file system, because what ends up in the file is the entire point of
the class.

Covered: the round trip, that whatever is saved reloads identically
including the done flag and every date field; that a missing file means
a first run rather than an error; that save creates the folder, since
it does not exist on a fresh clone; that an emptied list clears the
file instead of leaving stale contents; and each way a hand-edited line
can be wrong, checking it is skipped and counted while the good lines
around it still load. An unknown type letter gets its own test, because
guessing Todo there would turn damaged data into a task that looks
legitimate.

55 tests across five classes, all passing under gradlew test.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the JUnit test coverage target
commitResults.messageBody:
Record where tests live, how to run them, the naming convention, and
  the target of roughly the top 50% highest-value methods. State that
  tests are updated as part of any code change, so the project stays at
  that target rather than drifting once the increment is over.

commitResults.messageTitle: Comply with the SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The code was never checked against the standard the project is meant
to follow, so violations accumulated quietly while other increments
were being written.

An audit found the code already clean on indentation, line length,
tabs, wildcard imports, brace style, naming and package structure. Two
rules were broken. Ninety-three @param, @return and @throws
descriptions had no closing full stop. Two comments and one test method
name used British spelling, where the standard asks for American.

Add the missing full stops, and rename to behavior and Recognized. The
message shown when a command is not understood keeps its British
spelling: it is text shown to the user rather than a comment, so the
rule does not reach it, and changing it would alter program output for
no gain.

Verified with the audit commands in the seedu-java-coding-standard
skill, the 55 JUnit tests, and a scripted run of every command and
error path producing byte-identical output.

commitResults.messageTitle: Mandate the SE-EDU standards in AGENTS.md
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing in the project instructions told a contributor, human or AI,
which coding or commit standard to follow, so compliance depended on
whoever happened to remember.

Name both SE-EDU standards and point at the two project skills holding
them in full, then list the rules this codebase has actually broken so
they are visible without opening the skills.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command to search tasks by keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
A user with a long list had no way to pick out one task except reading
the whole list and counting, which gets worse the more the list is
used.

Add a find command that shows every task whose description contains a
keyword. Matching ignores case, since a user searching for "Book" means
the same thing as "book", and matches on part of a word so a partial
keyword still helps. Only the description is searched, which is what
the requirement asks for and keeps a date from matching by accident.

Each class answers for its own data: Task decides whether it matches,
TaskList collects the matches into a new list, and Ui prints them. The
matches are a separate list, so the real one keeps its numbering and
mark and delete still work off the numbers that list shows.

An empty keyword and a search with no matches are both reported through
the usual error channel, so a reply is never just a heading with
nothing under it.

Adds 14 JUnit tests, including a new TaskTest, for a suite of 69.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Checkstyle to enforce the coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The seedu-java-coding-standard skill is guidance applied while writing:
  nothing verifies it afterwards, and it omits several mechanical rules.

  Add Gradle's built-in Checkstyle plugin with the SE-EDU configuration.
  The two are complementary: the skill covers judgement the tool cannot
  make, such as whether a name explains its purpose, while the tool
  checks the whole codebase on every build.

  Fix the 53 violations this surfaced. None change behavior: case label
  indentation in switches, import order, one field declaration order,
  and a wrapped bracket in two tests.
